stereochem-001.question: Which of the following compounds contains an asymmetric carbon atom (chiral center)?
stereochem-001.explanation: An asymmetric carbon is an sp³ carbon bonded to four mutually different atoms or groups. C2 of 2-butanol carries four different groups, −H, −OH, −CH3 and −CH2CH3, so it is an asymmetric carbon, and a pair of enantiomers, the (R) and (S) forms, exists. C2 of 2-propanol carries two identical −CH3 groups, and in 1-propanol every carbon has at least two identical hydrogens, so neither has an asymmetric carbon. A molecule with exactly one asymmetric carbon is always chiral and cannot be superimposed on its mirror image.

stereochem-002.question: Which property has different values for two enantiomers (mirror-image isomers)?
choices: The direction in which they rotate plane-polarized light
stereochem-002.explanation: Enantiomers are mirror images of each other, with all interatomic distances and bond angles identical, so their melting points, boiling points and densities, their solubilities in achiral solvents such as water and hexane, and their IR and NMR spectra are all the same. Differences appear in interactions with something chiral: they rotate plane-polarized light by the same amount in opposite directions (specific rotations equal in magnitude and opposite in sign). They are also distinguished by chromatography on a chiral column and by binding to enzymes and receptors. A racemic crystal can have a melting point different from that of a pure enantiomer, but that is a property of the mixture.

stereochem-003.question: Under the CIP priority rules, which of the following substituents has the highest priority?
stereochem-003.explanation: The CIP rules first compare the atomic numbers of the atoms directly attached to the stereocenter. All three are carbon, so next you compare the sets of atoms attached to that carbon, listed in decreasing atomic number. −CH2Cl gives (Cl, H, H), −CH2OH gives (O, H, H) and −CH(CH3)2 gives (C, C, H); comparing the first atoms, Cl (17) > O (8) > C (6), so −CH2Cl is highest. Because a difference appears at this point, the second and later atoms are not compared. The isopropyl group has more carbons and is a "bigger" substituent, but priority is decided not by the number or size of atoms but by the atomic number at the first point of difference.

stereochem-004.question: Counting open-chain structures, how many stereoisomers are there of a straight-chain aldohexose, HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO (such as glucose)?
stereochem-004.explanation: In a straight-chain aldohexose, the four carbons C2–C5 are each stereocenters bearing −H, −OH and two different carbon chains. The two ends, CHO and CH2OH, differ, so the molecule has no symmetry and no meso forms arise, giving the maximum number of stereoisomers, 2⁴ = 16. These are the eight D sugars (glucose, mannose, galactose and others) and the eight L sugars that are their enantiomers. Eight counts only the D series, and four is the value you get by counting two stereocenters. In the cyclic (pyranose) form, C1 also becomes a new stereocenter (the anomeric carbon), adding the α/β distinction.

stereochem-005.question: How many stereoisomers of 2,3-dibromobutane, CH3CHBrCHBrCH3, are there in total?
stereochem-005.explanation: C2 and C3 are both stereocenters bearing −H, −Br, −CH3 and −CHBrCH3, so four combinations (2² = 4) are conceivable: (2R,3R), (2S,3S), (2R,3S) and (2S,3R). Because the two ends have the same structure, however, (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) can be superimposed thanks to an internal mirror plane and are the same meso compound. In the end there are three: the chiral enantiomeric pair (2R,3R) and (2S,3S), plus one achiral meso compound. Four applies 2ⁿ blindly, and two overlooks the meso compound. A meso compound has stereocenters but is not optically active.

stereochem-006.question: What is the relationship between the (2R,3R) and (2R,3S) isomers of 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane, CH3CHBrCHClCH3?
stereochem-006.explanation: Enantiomers are mirror images, with every stereocenter descriptor reversed; the enantiomer of (2R,3R) is (2S,3S). (2R,3S) differs at only one of the two stereocenters (C3), so it is a stereoisomer that is not a mirror image, that is, a diastereomer. In this molecule the substituents at C2 and C3 (Br and Cl) differ, so no meso form arises, and (2R,3S) cannot be identical to (2R,3R). Diastereomers differ in melting point, boiling point, solubility, NMR spectra and so on, so unlike enantiomers they can be separated by ordinary recrystallization, distillation or chromatography.

stereochem-007.question: The pure (+) enantiomer of a compound has a specific rotation of +40.0°. A sample measured under the same conditions has a specific rotation of +30.0°. What is the proportion of the (+) enantiomer in the sample (mol%)? Assume there are no impurities and that specific rotation is proportional to enantiomeric excess.
stereochem-007.explanation: The optical purity is 30.0/40.0 = 0.750, and if specific rotation is proportional to enantiomeric excess (ee), ee = 75.0%. Since ee = %(+) − %(−) and %(+) + %(−) = 100%, the (+) enantiomer is (100 + 75.0)/2 = 87.5% and the (−) enantiomer 12.5%. Viewing the sample as 75.0% pure (+) enantiomer plus 25.0% racemate (of which 12.5% is (+)) also gives 87.5% in total. 75.0% mistakes the ee for the proportion of the (+) enantiomer, and 12.5% is the proportion of the minor (−) enantiomer.

stereochem-008.question: A 5.00 g sample of a compound is dissolved in solvent to make 100 mL and measured at 20 °C with the sodium D line in a 20.0 cm cell, giving an observed rotation of +1.30°. What is the specific rotation [α]? Use [α] = α/(l·c), with l in dm and c in g/mL.
stereochem-008.explanation: The concentration is c = 5.00 g / 100 mL = 0.0500 g/mL and the cell length is l = 20.0 cm = 2.00 dm. [α] = α/(l·c) = 1.30 / (2.00 × 0.0500) = +13.0° (the units are deg·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹, but by convention it is often written with just "°"). +1.30° is what you get by using the cell length as 20.0 in cm; it happens to equal the observed value. +0.130° is what you get by using the concentration as 5.00 in g/100 mL. Specific rotation changes with temperature and wavelength, so always state the measurement conditions with it.

stereochem-009.question: The pure (R) enantiomer of a compound has a specific rotation of −50.0°. For a mixture of 80.0% (R) and 20.0% (S) (molar ratio), which pair gives the enantiomeric excess ee and the specific rotation? Assume specific rotation is proportional to ee.
stereochem-009.explanation: The ee is the proportion of the major enantiomer minus that of the minor one, 80.0 − 20.0 = 60.0%. The 20.0% of (S) cancels an equal 20.0% of (R) to make 40.0% racemate, and only the remaining 60.0% of (R) contributes to the rotation. The specific rotation is −50.0° × 0.600 = −30.0°. ee 80.0% with −40.0° ignores the cancellation and uses the proportion of (R) directly, and +30.0° flips the sign. That the (R) enantiomer is levorotatory (−) is a given fact about this compound; there is no general correspondence between the R/S descriptor and the sign of rotation.

stereochem-010.question: Which correctly describes the relationship between the R/S (CIP) descriptor and the direction in which plane-polarized light is rotated (+/−)?
choices: An R enantiomer is always dextrorotatory (+)
An R enantiomer is always levorotatory (−)
There is no general correspondence between the two; the direction of rotation is determined by measurement
stereochem-010.explanation: R/S is a naming convention determined mechanically from substituent priorities and spatial arrangement, while the direction of optical rotation (+/−) is a physical quantity obtained by actually measuring polarized light. The two are independent: for example, oxidizing dextrorotatory (R)-glyceraldehyde gives (R)-glyceric acid, which is levorotatory. Even for the same compound, the sign of rotation can change with solvent, pH and measurement wavelength. The D/L descriptors used for sugars and amino acids are also based on the arrangement in a Fischer projection and have nothing to do with the direction of rotation. So both choices claiming that an R enantiomer is always dextrorotatory or always levorotatory are wrong.

stereochem-011.question: A stereocenter is viewed with its lowest-priority substituent (H) pointing toward the viewer, and the remaining substituents run clockwise in priority order 1→2→3. What is the descriptor of this stereocenter?
choices: It cannot be determined from this information alone
stereochem-011.explanation: In the CIP rules, you view the stereocenter with the lowest-priority substituent pointing away from you; if 1→2→3 runs clockwise it is R, and if counterclockwise, S. With the lowest-priority group pointing toward you, you are looking from the opposite side, so the sense of rotation appears reversed. An apparent clockwise sequence is therefore counterclockwise from the correct direction, giving S. Answering R from what you see is the classic mistake. Once you know the direction of the lowest-priority group and the sense of rotation, the descriptor is fixed uniquely, so "cannot be determined" is also wrong. A handy rule: when H is on a wedge (toward you), just reverse the result you get.

stereochem-012.question: Which of the following compounds is chiral (exists as a pair of enantiomers)?
stereochem-012.explanation: C1 and C2 of 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane are both stereocenters. In the cis isomer, the two methyl groups are on the same side of the ring, and there is a mirror plane perpendicular to the ring passing through C3 and the midpoint of the C1−C2 bond, so it is a meso compound (achiral) that is superimposable on its mirror image. The trans isomer has neither a mirror plane nor a center of symmetry and exists as the enantiomeric pair (1R,2R) and (1S,2S), so it is chiral. 1,1-Dimethylcyclopropane has no stereocenter, and the plane of the ring itself is a mirror plane, so it is achiral. It is important to judge not only by whether stereocenters are present but by whether the whole molecule has a mirror plane.

stereochem-013.question: Of the two chair conformations of methylcyclohexane, which is more stable, and why?
choices: The conformation with the methyl group equatorial, because in the axial position it suffers 1,3-diaxial interactions with the axial hydrogens at C3 and C5
The conformation with the methyl group axial, because the methyl group points away from the plane of the ring and steric repulsion is small
The two conformations are equal in energy, and each is present at 50%
stereochem-013.explanation: In the chair form of cyclohexane, ring flipping interchanges axial and equatorial substituents. An axial methyl group comes close to the axial hydrogens at C3 and C5 on the same side of the ring, causing steric repulsion (1,3-diaxial interactions). The equatorial conformation is more stable by about 7.3 kJ/mol in Gibbs energy, and at 25 °C about 95% is present in the equatorial conformation. Axial bonds are perpendicular to the mean plane of the ring and approach substituents on the same side, so the idea that they point "away" is backward. A large substituent such as tert-butyl is locked almost completely in the equatorial position.

stereochem-014.question: In methylcyclohexane, the conformation with the methyl group equatorial is more stable than the axial one by 7.3 kJ/mol in Gibbs energy. Which value is closest to the fraction of the equatorial conformation at equilibrium at 25 °C (298 K)? Take the gas constant R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
stereochem-014.explanation: The equilibrium constant is K = [equatorial]/[axial] = exp(−ΔG°/RT) (ΔG° = −7300 J/mol for axial → equatorial) = exp(7300 / (8.314 × 298)) = exp(2.95) ≈ 19. The fraction of the equatorial conformation is K/(1 + K) = 19/20 ≈ 0.95, or about 95%. About 5% is the fraction of the minor axial conformation. About 99.9% comes from computing a power of ten instead of exp, 10^2.95 ≈ 890. At room temperature the ring flips more than 100,000 times a second, so the two conformations cannot be separated and exist as an equilibrium mixture.

stereochem-015.question: Which of the following dimethylcyclohexanes can place both methyl groups equatorial in a chair conformation?
stereochem-015.explanation: At the 1,4-positions, two substituents on the same side of the ring (cis) are one axial and one equatorial (a,e), while two on opposite sides (trans) are either both equatorial (e,e) or both axial (a,a). The trans-1,4 isomer can therefore adopt the e,e conformation, which is very stable. At the 1,3-positions the relationship is reversed: the cis isomer is e,e and the trans isomer a,e. At the 1,2-positions, trans is e,e and cis is a,e. In both cis-1,4 and trans-1,3, one methyl group is axial in either conformation. The way the cis/trans to a/e correspondence switches with position is an easy place to go wrong.
